title: Balanced Bit Blocks
statement:
You get a string s made only of the characters '0' and '1'.

Count the non-empty substrings (contiguous pieces) that contain the same number of 0s and 1s, and in which all the 0s sit together and all the 1s sit together. So "0011" and "10" count, but "0101" does not.

Substrings at different positions are counted separately, even when they spell the same text.

examples.why: The pieces are "01" and "0011" around the first switch, and "10" and "1100" around the second. "011100" is not balanced: three 1s against three 0s, but the 0s are split.
"01", "10" and "01" again at a new position. The whole string has two of each, but its 0s are not in one block, so it does not count.
There is no 0 to balance any 1.

hints: Every valid substring has exactly one place where the character switches. Look at the string as a list of runs, like 000 11 0.
Take two neighbouring runs of lengths a and b. How many valid substrings straddle the border between them?
Exactly min(a, b): one for each size from 1 up to the shorter run. Sum that over every pair of neighbouring runs, keeping only the previous run's length.

explain.intuition:
A valid substring is some 0s followed by the same number of 1s, or the other way round. So it always crosses exactly one border between two runs, and it is centred on that border.

Take a border between a run of length a and a run of length b. You can take 1 character from each side, or 2 from each side, and so on, until one side runs out. That is min(a, b) substrings. Different borders give different substrings, so the answer is the sum of min(prev, cur) over all neighbouring runs. You only ever need the previous run's length and the current one.
steps: Walk i from 1 to the end. If s[i] equals s[i − 1], the current run grows: cur++.
Otherwise a run just ended: add min(prev, cur) to total, then prev = cur, cur = 1.
After the loop add min(prev, cur) once more for the last border, and return total.
pitfalls: Counting every substring with equal 0s and 1s. "0101" is balanced but its 0s are split, so it must not count.
Forgetting the final border after the loop ends. In "0001" the only border is right before the last character.
Adding max(a, b) or a + b for a border. A substring needs the same count on both sides, so the shorter run limits it.

solutions.title: Grow from every start
solutions.idea: From each start, extend to the right while there is at most one switch, and count the moments when the two counts are equal.

solutions.title: Run lengths, two at a time
solutions.idea: Each border between neighbouring runs of lengths a and b contributes min(a, b). Keep only the previous and current run lengths.

followups: The string has three letters and a valid substring is a block of each in a fixed order, all the same length. How does the run idea extend?
Answer the same question for many ranges [l, r] of one long string. What would you precompute?
